hints: Look at what changes from ethanol to ethanoic acid and think which strong oxidising agent supplies oxygen for full oxidation to the acid.
Think about the conditions needed to keep the volatile alcohol in contact with the oxidiser long enough for two stages of oxidation without loss.
walkthrough:
Spot how far the oxidation goes**
You start with $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, a primary alcohol, and you finish with $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, a carboxylic acid. That is full oxidation, not stopping at ethanal. So you need a strong oxidiser that can provide plenty of $\text{[O]}$.

Pick the classic AS oxidiser**
For primary alcohol to carboxylic acid, memorise this pair: potassium or sodium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, acidified with dilute sulfuric acid. Acid is essential for the dichromate to work as an oxidiser.

Lock in the condition**
Ethanol and ethanal both boil easily and would escape. Heating under reflux condenses vapours and returns them to the flask, so the alcohol stays with the hot oxidiser long enough to be oxidised fully to ethanoic acid.

Final answer: reagent(s): acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ (sodium dichromate also allowed)
conditions: heat under reflux

hints: Count atoms on each side starting from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and see how many $\text{[O]}$ and water molecules balance H and O.
walkthrough:
Balance with [O] as the oxidiser**
Write the carbon skeleton first: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. To balance O and H, you need two atoms of oxygen from the oxidiser and you make one water as well: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2[\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check: 3 O each side, 6 H each side.

hints: Compare $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ with $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and notice which atom has been swapped for bromine.
walkthrough:
See the swap**
Look closely: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{BrCH}_2\text{COOH}$. One H on the methyl group has been replaced by one Br. When one atom takes the place of another with nothing else added to the skeleton, that is substitution.

hints: Recall the meaning of homo as same and think about the physical states of the acid catalyst and the liquid organic reactants in reaction 3.
walkthrough:
Unpack the word homogeneous**
Homo means same. A homogeneous catalyst does its job while mixed in the same phase as the reactants. Here $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ dissolves in the liquid reaction mixture, so catalyst and reactants are all in one liquid phase, not on a separate solid surface.
Final answer: Homogeneous because $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is in the same phase / same state as the reactants.

hints: Think what product forms when compound C, which has both $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{OH}$, reacts with ethanol in reaction 3 conditions.
Use the Data Booklet values to match the two strong IR bands at $1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and $1720 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ to specific bonds.
Check what is missing in the IR of D compared with C, especially the broad absorption for hydrogen bonded O-H.
walkthrough:
Picture what D must be**
C is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. It has a carboxylic acid end and an alcohol end. With ethanol and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, both ends can esterify. D is said to have two identical functional groups, so both ends have become the same ester linkage.

Match the two strong bands**
Open your Data Booklet. A strong band at $1720 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the classic C=O stretch of an ester, and a strong band at $1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the C-O stretch of an ester. Seeing both together points strongly to ester, not just a ketone or ether alone.

Use the missing band as proof**
C would show a very broad O-H band from its $\text{COOH}$ and its alcohol $\text{OH}$. D shows no absorption due to O-H bonds. That tells you those $\text{OH}$ and $\text{COOH}$ groups are gone, they have reacted to form ester links. No O-H plus C=O plus C-O equals ester.

Final answer: Functional group in D is ester.
$1100 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ corresponds to C-O and $1720 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ corresponds to C=O, both present in an ester.
No O-H absorption shows the $\text{COOH}$ and $\text{OH}$ groups of C have reacted / been lost, consistent with ester formation.

hints: Remember which group in C reacts with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ and which group is left untouched.
walkthrough:
Let only the acid react**
C has $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ is a base that neutralises the carboxylic acid but leaves the alcohol $\text{OH}$ alone. So you swap the acidic H for Na to give the carboxylate salt: $$\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH} \rightarrow \text{HOCH}_2\text{COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$$ which is written $\text{NaOCOCH}_2\text{OH}$.

hints: Think about what functional group must be reduced to turn C into the diol F, and recall the limit of $\text{NaBH}_4$ compared with $\text{LiAlH}_4$.
walkthrough:
See the reduction needed**
To go from $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$ to $\text{(CH}_2\text{OH)}_2$, the $\text{COOH}$ must be reduced to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. $\text{NaBH}_4$ is a mild reducing agent, it handles aldehydes and ketones but it cannot reduce a carboxylic acid. You would need the stronger $\text{LiAlH}_4$ for that change.
Final answer: $\text{NaBH}_4$ is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce the carboxylic acid (to a primary alcohol).

hints: Write the diol as $(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2$ and replace each $\text{OH}$ by $\text{Cl}$ to give G, then add the usual $\text{SOCl}_2$ byproducts $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as given.
walkthrough:
Build the chlorination equation**
$\text{SOCl}_2$ swaps each alcohol $\text{OH}$ for $\text{Cl}$. So the diol $(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2$ becomes the dichloride $(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl})_2$. Balance with the expected byproducts: $$(\text{CH}_2\text{OH})_2 + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow (\text{CH}_2\text{Cl})_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Look at the two oxygen containing groups in C and think what type of intermolecular attraction they can set up with water molecules.
walkthrough:
Link the groups to water**
C, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$, is small and packed with hydrogen bonding sites: the alcohol $\text{OH}$ and the carboxylic acid $\text{COOH}$. Both can donate and accept hydrogen bonds with surrounding water molecules. Those strong solute to solvent attractions release energy and pull C into solution, giving very high solubility.
Final answer: C is very soluble because it forms hydrogen bonds with water.
